metadata.narrative: How much should we (the current generation) have to change our lives to tackle climate change for for future generations? I want you to 1. explain and compare at least two ethical frameworks (eg utilitarianism, deontology, contractualism) that address duties to future people 2. discuss the concept of non-identity problem and its implications for climate ethics 3. evaluate real-world policies (eg carbon taxes, intergenerational equity acts) that try to codify long-term responsibility 4. reference at least one philosophical source and one empirical policy example 5. address possible counterarguments, like claims about discounting the future or epistemic uncertainty
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: The question of how much the present generation must sacrifice for those not yet born sits at the center of climate ethics, and philosophers approach it through competing frameworks that disagree about why future people matter and how much weight their interests deserve.

Classical utilitarianism holds that equal moral weight should be attached to the welfare of every person, present or future, so that suffering imposed on someone born in 2100 counts exactly as much as suffering imposed on someone alive today.

Against this, "presentism" denies that future generations possess full moral standing and grounds obligations to descendants merely in the altruistic preferences current people already hold toward their children and grandchildren, setting a lower, more contingent bar for sacrifice.

A rights-based approach argues future people are entitled to protection from harm because all persons possess basic rights to life, health, and subsistence, a view built on a "no-harm principle" that forbids imposing avoidable harm where viable alternatives like renewables exist.

Contractualist approaches add a fourth lens: Rawls's original position asks what principles people would choose behind a "veil of ignorance" hiding which generation they belong to, requiring preservation of just institutions across generations rather than mere welfare maximization.
Scanlon's contractualism differs by asking whether a rule could be reasonably rejected by anyone affected, grounding duties in mutual respect rather than a hypothetical bargain.

These frameworks converge on owing the future something but diverge sharply on how much: utilitarian aggregation can demand large present sacrifices if future benefits are larger still, while rights-based and contractualist views set firmer floors that cost-benefit calculation cannot override.
The non-identity problem complicates all these frameworks by undermining the idea that our climate choices "harm" specific future individuals.
Parfit observed that many of our actions affect not just future welfare but future identity itself, since different energy policies lead to different people being conceived altogether.

In the classic illustration, building a coal plant rather than a wind farm changes who is born, so the resulting child cannot be worse off "than he would otherwise have been," since in the alternative he would not exist, a point echoed by McMahan's observation that policies degrading future quality of life cannot be criticized as against any particular person's interests.

Parfit extended this directly to environmental policy by comparing "Depletion," which exhausts resources for short-term gain, against "Conservation," showing that because the two policies produce entirely different future populations, no specific person can claim Depletion made them worse off, even though most people intuitively judge it wrong.

This has pushed philosophers toward "impersonal" reasons for action, meaning outcomes can be good or bad in aggregate even absent an identifiable victim, a view roughly three-quarters of surveyed readers implicitly endorsed when judging Depletion wrong.

Finneron-Burns offers a contractarian response distinguishing "wronging" from "harming," arguing we can wrong future people through unfair treatment even without harming any specific individual, by evaluating duties toward categories of future persons rather than particular undetermined individuals.

The upshot is that arguments resting purely on "don't harm identifiable victims" are vulnerable to the non-identity objection, so durable climate obligations likely require impersonal or rights-based reasoning rather than person-affecting harm alone.
Turning to real policy, carbon taxes are the most direct attempt to price intergenerational harm into present decisions, and Sweden's three-decade experience is the most tested case.
Sweden implemented its carbon tax in 1991 and now levies the world's highest rate, about $126 per ton of CO2, while cutting emissions 27 percent between 1990 and 2018 alongside continued GDP growth.

Critics note the tax covers only about 40 percent of national emissions because exemptions and caps let the largest industrial polluters escape marginal incentives, showing that even a strong carbon price can underperform its ethical promise once political compromise carves out big emitters.

A second strategy codifies intergenerational duty directly into law, as with the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015, which sets statutory wellbeing goals, requires public bodies to safeguard the long term, and creates a Future Generations Commissioner to advocate for people not yet born.

Internationally, the Paris Agreement commits 195 nations to respect "intergenerational equity," language that has since supported rights litigation such as the US Juliana lawsuit invoking government duty to secure liberty's "blessings" to "our Posterity."

A third lever is the social discount rate used in cost-benefit analysis: a 2021 survey found philosophers and economists converging near 2 percent, a figure with major stakes, since raising the US rate from 3 to 7 percent cuts the social cost of carbon sevenfold, while New York's move from 3 to 2 percent raised its social cost of carbon from $40 to $125 per ton.
Two counterarguments recur against demanding present sacrifice.

The discounting objection holds future costs should count for less than present ones, but the philosopher-economist consensus around a low 2 percent rate is explicitly grounded in intergenerational fairness rather than pure impatience, undercutting harsher discounting historically used to minimize climate costs.
The epistemic-uncertainty objection holds that because catastrophic outcomes cannot be assigned precise probabilities, policymakers should wait for more certainty before imposing costly change.

Gardiner answers with a Rawlsian "playing it safe" argument: under genuine "strong uncertainty" about tipping points, a maximin rule favors precaution because the worst case of inaction is far graver than the worst case of unnecessary precautionary spending.

This mirrors the precautionary principle formalized in the 1992 Rio Declaration and 1998 Wingspread Statement, both insisting scientific uncertainty must not become a reason for inaction where serious or irreversible harm is plausible.

Some ethicists argue the burden of proof should reverse entirely, since the "no-harm principle" already obligates governments to avoid transboundary harm, even though scientific-uncertainty rhetoric has dominated policy debate for roughly forty years.

Taken together, these frameworks and policies suggest the current generation cannot treat uncertainty or discounting as license for inaction, though genuine disagreement remains about whether obligations are best pitched as rights-based floors, contractualist fairness, or utilitarian aggregation, leaving the precise scale of required sacrifice a matter of ongoing dispute.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

The question of how much the present generation must sacrifice for those not yet born sits at the center of climate ethics, and philosophers have approached it through competing frameworks that disagree sharply about why future people matter and how much weight their interests deserve.

Classical utilitarianism holds that equal moral weight should be attached to the welfare of every person, present or future, so that a ton of carbon-driven suffering imposed on someone born in 2100 counts exactly as much as suffering imposed on someone alive today. [shard_05759_43632]
Against this, "presentism" denies that future generations possess full moral standing and instead grounds obligations to descendants in the altruistic preferences current people already hold toward their own children and grandchildren, which sets a much lower and more contingent bar for sacrifice. [shard_05759_43632]
A third, rights-based approach argues that future people are entitled to protection from harm simply because all persons, regardless of when they are born, possess basic rights to life, health, and subsistence that climate change threatens, a view associated with philosophers Simon Caney and Henry Shue and built on a "no-harm principle" that forbids imposing avoidable harm when viable alternatives like renewable energy exist. [shard_00351_81044]
Contractualist approaches offer a fourth lens: John Rawls's original position asks what principles people would choose behind a "veil of ignorance" that hides which generation they belong to, and his framework requires establishing and preserving just institutions across generations rather than merely maximizing aggregate welfare. [shard_04405_78627]
Thomas Scanlon's version of contractualism differs from Rawls by asking whether a rule or action could be reasonably rejected by anyone affected by it, grounding duties in mutual respect and reciprocity among rational agents rather than in a hypothetical bargaining position. [shard_03658_11806]
These frameworks converge on the conclusion that some sacrifice is owed to the future, but they diverge on how much: utilitarian aggregation can, in principle, demand very large present sacrifices if they produce even larger future benefits, whereas presentism counsels modest, preference-based transfers, and rights-based and contractualist views set firmer, threshold-style floors below which no cost-benefit calculation can push future people's basic entitlements. [shard_05759_43632] [shard_00351_81044]

The non-identity problem complicates all of these frameworks by undermining the very idea that our climate choices "harm" specific future individuals.
Philosopher Derek Parfit observed that many of our actions affect not just the welfare of future people but their very identity, since different energy policies lead to different couples meeting, different children being conceived, and therefore different people existing altogether. [shard_03488_17544]
In the classic illustration, building a coal plant rather than a wind farm changes who is born, so the child born into the coal-powered world cannot be said to be "worse off than he would otherwise have been," because in the alternative scenario he simply would not exist, a point echoed by philosopher Jeff McMahan's observation that policies degrading the far future's quality of life cannot be criticized as against the interests of the particular people who will live then. [shard_03488_17544]
